Md. Rezaul Karim alias Rezaul
Vs.

full_judgment:
7. Mr. Sarwar Ahmed the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant after taking us through the entire evidence on record specially the depositions made by the witnesses and other related things has submitted that prosecution in the instant case could not prove the allegation against the accused-appellant beyond all reasonable doubt. The learned counsel has pointed out that this is a case where the accused-appellant will get the benefit of doubt. Substantiating his argument the learned counsel further submits that admittedly the occurrence took place at night and it was dark all over and also drizzling therefore it was not possible to recognize the appellant by the victim as there was no means of recognition. Next he submits that PWs. 1. 2. 3. 4 and 6 are all relatives of the informant who are partisan witnesses and as such their evidences are not worthy of credit. Besides withdrawing of neighbouring witness specially Muzibur Rahman in front of whose house the incident took place was not examined gives rise to a presumption under section 114G of the Evidence Act. He further contends that on the basis of the defence suggestion conviction cannot be given. On this point he placed reliance on 6 BLD (AD)1 and 15 BLD(AD)54. The learned counsel in support of his other contentions as stated above cited so many decisions. On the point of recognition, 15 BLD121, 11 BLT 267 and on the point of interested and partisan witness 15 BLD(AD)54, 57 DLR(AD)277 and on the point of withdrawing of witness within the meaning of section 114G of the Evidence Act 48 DLR(AD)196, 57 DLR(AD)513 were cited. Summing up his argument the learned counsel submits that it is a fit case where benefit of doubt should have been given to the accused appellant and he should have been acquitted. 

 27. We have gone through the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence, evidence on record, specially the deposition of the prosecution witnesses, memo of appeal, FIR, charge sheet, charge and other related documents of the case in details and carefully. We have also heard the learned counsel for the appellant at length. In this case prosecution has produced as many as 16 witnesses out of which PWs.5 and 10-13 were tendered by the prosecution and declined by the defence for cross-examination. P.W.8 was declared hostile, and rest of the witnesses are vital witnesses of whom victim deposed as P.W.2. If we critically discuss the whole case we find that admittedly the victim David sustained an acid burning injury on the date of occurrence. P.W.1 father of the victim who is the informant categorically in his deposition stated that immediately after the occurrence hearing hue and cry of the victim he rushed to the place of occurrence and heard from his son, the victim, how he sustained acid burning injury by the accused-appellant Rezaul P.Ws. 4 and 6 also corroborated P.W.1 the informant and stated that immediately after the occurrence they came to the spot and heard from the victim about the occurrence P.Ws. 3. 7 and 8 stated that they heard about the occurrence which took place on that night. P.W.2 is the victim who gave a vivid and graphic description of the heinous and detestable act inflicted upon him on the fateful night. He stared that he sustained acid injury caused by the accused-appellant Rezaul. We do not find any earthly reason to disbelieve this natural and voluntary statement given by him implicating the accused-appellant and none else for the same. From the facts and circumstances of the case a reasonable and plausible presumption could be made why of all the persons he would mention the name of the accused-appellant Rezaul. It is also relevant in this respect to quote the observations made by the learned Judge of the Tribunal basing on the decision of Ataur Rahman and others Vs. The State reported in 43 DLR 87 that an injured person in natural course of event will tell the name of the person who has inflicted the injury. In that decision it was observed, 

 31. Regarding withholding of the vital witnesses as pointed out in the present case by the learned counsel we record that the law is very clear on this point. As a general rule prosecution would examine only those witnesses which they will deem necessary and important for the purpose. Regard may be taken to the decision reported in 9BLC (AD) 122. Moreover section 134 of the Evidence Act laid down the golden principle that conviction can be based upon the solitary testimony of the witness if it is worthy of credit. So the question of presumption of withholding the evidence within the meaning of section 114(G) of the Evidence Act is of no avail in the present case. We find that in order to prove its case the prosecution left no stone unturned to bring the necessary and important witnesses for that purpose. The decision reported in the case of Shamsul Huq and others Vs. The State reported in 6 BLD 216 is also on the same point.
